content.text:
lets iteratively build our way up to a PAAS

I want to build a self host PAAS to host non-production apps (demo, experimental apps) in an enterprise environment.

The PAAS will probably be hosted in GCP in an account dedicated to non-production use

The PAAS apps should be language agnostic  (Container implied)
The PAAS should provide the ability to run apps that are some combination of

* HTTP servers
* Workers
* Scheduled jobs
The PAAS must provide persistence for apps in the form of

* Blob storage
* Databases
* Queues
The PAAS must be able to make its apps unreachable from the public internet
The PAAS must be able to manage DNS and HTTPS for its apps (under some domain managed by the operator)
The PAAS must be able to wholly manage its apps via git ops (IAC implied)
The PAAS must be multi-user (the users are expected to be members of a private github org managed by the operator)

It must be low maintenance (part time maintenance for a single operator)
It must implement cost caps (implies quotas for individual users or apps)
It must be able to detect and hibernate apps that have not been used for a while
It must be able to transfer ownership of apps (as people leave the github org)

Let use these requirements as a starting point and gather more as we go
This is a well-scoped problem. Before diving into architecture, let me ask a few things that will significantly shape the design:

options: Small: ~5 users, ~20 apps
Medium: ~20 users, ~100 apps
Large: ~50+ users, ~500+ apps
questions.question: How many apps and users are you expecting at steady state?

options: Minimal: prefer managed services (Cloud Run, etc.)
Moderate: okay with GKE if it buys flexibility
High: fine with full Kubernetes control plane
questions.question: How much GCP infrastructure complexity are you comfortable managing?

options: Push to git → auto deploy (Heroku-style)
PR-based: deploy on merge to main
Explicit: deploy command / manifest in repo
questions.question: How do developers deploy apps — what's your preferred GitOps model?

content.text:
Q: How many apps and users are you expecting at steady state?
A: Large: ~50+ users, ~500+ apps

Q: How much GCP infrastructure complexity are you comfortable managing?
A: High: fine with full Kubernetes control plane

Q: How do developers deploy apps — what's your preferred GitOps model?
A: Push to git → auto deploy (Heroku-style)

Good answers — these significantly clarify the architecture. Large scale + full K8s + Heroku-style DX points to a clear stack. Let me lay out the overall design before we start building anything iteratively.

# Imagine — Visual Creation Suite ## Modules Call read_me again with the modules parameter to load detailed guidance: - `diagram` — SVG flowcharts, structural diagrams, illustrative diagrams - `mockup` — UI mockups, forms, cards, dashboards - `interactive` — interactive explainers with controls - `chart` — charts, data analysis, geographic maps (Chart.js, D3 choropleth) - `art` — illustration and generative art Pick the closest fit. The module includes all relevant design guidance. **Complexity budget — hard limits:** - Box subtitles: ≤5 words. Detail goes in click-through (`sendPrompt`) or the prose below — not the box. - Colors: ≤2 ramps per diagram. If colors encode meaning (states, tiers), add a 1-line legend. Otherwise use one neutral ramp. - Horizontal tier: ≤4 boxes at full width (~140px each). 5+ boxes → shrink to ≤110px OR wrap to 2 rows OR split into overview + detail diagrams. If you catch yourself writing "click to learn more" in prose, the diagram itself must ACTUALLY be sparse. Don't promise brevity then front-load everything. **Accessibility:** For HTML widgets, begin with a visually-hidden `

` containing a one-sentence summary of the visualization for screen-reader users. (SVG widgets use `role="img"` with `` and `<desc>` instead — see SVG setup.) You create rich visual content — SVG diagrams/illustrations and HTML interactive widgets — that renders inline in conversation. The best output feels like a natural extension of the chat. ## Core Design System These rules apply to ALL use cases. ### Philosophy - **Seamless**: Users shouldn't notice where claude.ai ends and your widget begins. - **Flat**: No gradients, mesh backgrounds, noise textures, or decorative effects. Clean flat surfaces. - **Compact**: Show the essential inline. Explain the rest in text. - **Text goes in your response, visuals go in the tool** — All explanatory text, descriptions, introductions, and summaries must be written as normal response text OUTSIDE the tool call. The tool output should contain ONLY the visual element (diagram, chart, interactive widget). Never put paragraphs of explanation, section headings, or descriptive prose inside the HTML/SVG. If the user asks "explain X", write the explanation in your response and use the tool only for the visual that accompanies it. The user's font settings only apply to your response text, not to text inside the widget. ### Streaming Output streams token-by-token. Structure code so useful content appears early. - **HTML**: `<style>` (short) → content HTML → `<script>` last. - **SVG**: `<defs>` (markers) → visual elements immediately. - Prefer inline `style="..."` over `<style>` blocks — inputs/controls must look correct mid-stream. - Keep `<style>` under ~15 lines. Interactive widgets with inputs and sliders need more style rules — that's fine, but don't bloat with decorative CSS. - Gradients, shadows, and blur flash during streaming DOM diffs. Use solid flat fills instead. ### Rules - No `<!-- comments -->` or `/* comments */` (waste tokens, break streaming) - No font-size below 11px - No emoji. Icons = Tabler **outline** webfont (5800+, already loaded): `<i class="ti ti-home"></i>`. Outline only — never use `-filled` suffixes (`ti-heart-filled` etc. are not loaded and will render blank). Inherits color + font-size from parent. Decorative icons get `aria-hidden="true"`; icon-only buttons get `aria-label`. Common: ti-home ti-settings ti-user ti-search ti-x ti-check ti-plus ti-trash ti-edit ti-download ti-upload ti-file ti-folder ti-chart-bar ti-calendar ti-clock ti-arrow-right ti-arrow-left ti-chevron-down ti-external-link ti-copy ti-refresh ti-player-play ti-player-pause ti-heart ti-star ti-bell ti-mail ti-lock ti-eye ti-menu-2. Don't hand-draw icon SVG paths. - No gradients, drop shadows, blur, glow, or neon effects - No dark/colored backgrounds on outer containers (transparent only — host provides the bg) - **Typography**: The default font is Anthropic Sans. For the rare editorial/blockquote moment, use `font-family: var(--font-serif)`. - **Headings**: h1 = 22px, h2 = 18px, h3 = 16px — all `font-weight: 500`. Heading color is pre-set to `var(--color-text-primary)` — don't override it. Body text = 16px, weight 400, `line-height: 1.7`. **Two weights only: 400 regular, 500 bold.** Never use 600 or 700 — they look heavy against the host UI. - **Sentence case** always. Never Title Case, never ALL CAPS. This applies everywhere including SVG text labels and diagram headings. - **No mid-sentence bolding**, including in your response text around the tool call. Entity names, class names, function names go in `code style` not **bold**. Bold is for headings and labels only. - The widget container is `display: block; width: 100%`. Your HTML fills it naturally — no wrapper div needed. Just start with your content directly. If you want vertical breathing room, add `padding: 1rem 0` on your first element. - Never use `position: fixed` — the iframe viewport sizes itself to your in-flow content height, so fixed-positioned elements (modals, overlays, tooltips) collapse it to `min-height: 100px`. For modal/overlay mockups: wrap everything in a normal-flow `<div style="min-height: 400px; background: rgba(0,0,0,0.45); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;">` and put the modal inside — it's a faux viewport that actually contributes layout height. - No DOCTYPE, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` — just content fragments. - When placing text on a colored background (badges, pills, cards, tags), use the darkest shade from that same color family for the text — never plain black or generic gray. - **Corners**: use `border-radius: var(--border-radius-md)` (or `-lg` for cards) in HTML. In SVG, `rx="4"` is the default — larger values make pills, use only when you mean a pill. - **No rounded corners on single-sided borders** — if using `border-left` or `border-top` accents, set `border-radius: 0`. Rounded corners only work with full borders on all sides. - **No titles or prose inside the tool output** — see Philosophy above. - **Icon sizing**: Tabler `<i class="ti …">` sizes with `font-size` — 16–20px inline, 24px max decorative. For one-off inline SVG icons, set `width`/`height` explicitly (same limits). - No tabs, carousels, or `display: none` sections during streaming — hidden content streams invisibly. Show all content stacked vertically. (Post-streaming JS-driven steppers are fine — see Illustrative/Interactive sections.) - No nested scrolling — auto-fit height. - Scripts execute after streaming — load libraries via `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` (UMD globals), then use the global in a plain `<script>` that follows. - **CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external resources may ONLY load from `cdnjs.cloudflare.com`, `esm.sh`, `cdn.jsdelivr.net`, `unpkg.com`. All other origins are blocked by the sandbox — the request silently fails. ### CSS Variables **Backgrounds**: `--color-background-primary` (white), `-secondary` (surfaces), `-tertiary` (page bg), `-info`, `-danger`, `-success`, `-warning` **Text**: `--color-text-primary` (black), `-secondary` (muted), `-tertiary` (hints), `-info`, `-danger`, `-success`, `-warning` **Borders**: `--color-border-tertiary` (0.15α, default), `-secondary` (0.3α, hover), `-primary` (0.4α), semantic `-info/-danger/-success/-warning` **Typography**: `--font-sans`, `--font-serif`, `--font-mono` **Layout**: `--border-radius-md` (8px), `--border-radius-lg` (12px — preferred for most components), `--border-radius-xl` (16px) All auto-adapt to light/dark mode. For custom colors in HTML, use CSS variables. **Dark mode is mandatory** — every color must work in both modes: - In SVG: use the pre-built color classes (`c-blue`, `c-teal`, `c-amber`, etc.) for colored nodes — they handle light/dark mode automatically. Never write `<style>` blocks for colors. - In SVG: every `<text>` element needs a class (`t`, `ts`, `th`) — never omit fill or use `fill="inherit"`. Inside a `c-{color}` parent, text classes auto-adjust to the ramp. - In HTML: always use CSS variables (--color-text-primary, --color-text-secondary) for text. Never hardcode colors like color: #333 — invisible in dark mode. - Mental test: if the background were near-black, would every text element still be readable? ### sendPrompt(text) A global function that sends a message to chat as if the user typed it. Use it when the user's next step benefits from Claude thinking. Handle filtering, sorting, toggling, and calculations in JS instead. ### Links `<a href="https://...">` just works — clicks are intercepted and open the host's link-confirmation dialog. Or call `openLink(url)` directly. ## When nothing fits Pick the closest use case below and adapt. When nothing fits cleanly: - Default to editorial layout if the content is explanatory - Default to card layout if the content is a bounded object - All core design system rules still apply - Use `sendPrompt()` for any action that benefits from Claude thinking ## Color palette 9 color ramps, each with 7 stops from lightest to darkest. 50 = lightest fill, 100-200 = light fills, 400 = mid tones, 600 = strong/border, 800-900 = text on light fills. | Class | Ramp | 50 (lightest) | 100 | 200 | 400 | 600 | 800 | 900 (darkest) | |-------|------|------|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|------| | `c-purple` | Purple | #EEEDFE | #CECBF6 | #AFA9EC | #7F77DD | #534AB7 | #3C3489 | #26215C | | `c-teal` | Teal | #E1F5EE | #9FE1CB | #5DCAA5 | #1D9E75 | #0F6E56 | #085041 | #04342C | | `c-coral` | Coral | #FAECE7 | #F5C4B3 | #F0997B | #D85A30 | #993C1D | #712B13 | #4A1B0C | | `c-pink` | Pink | #FBEAF0 | #F4C0D1 | #ED93B1 | #D4537E | #993556 | #72243E | #4B1528 | | `c-gray` | Gray | #F1EFE8 | #D3D1C7 | #B4B2A9 | #888780 | #5F5E5A | #444441 | #2C2C2A | | `c-blue` | Blue | #E6F1FB | #B5D4F4 | #85B7EB | #378ADD | #185FA5 | #0C447C | #042C53 | | `c-green` | Green | #EAF3DE | #C0DD97 | #97C459 | #639922 | #3B6D11 | #27500A | #173404 | | `c-amber` | Amber | #FAEEDA | #FAC775 | #EF9F27 | #BA7517 | #854F0B | #633806 | #412402 | | `c-red` | Red | #FCEBEB | #F7C1C1 | #F09595 | #E24B4A | #A32D2D | #791F1F | #501313 | **How to assign colors**: Color should encode meaning, not sequence. Don't cycle through colors like a rainbow (step 1 = blue, step 2 = amber, step 3 = red...). Instead: - Group nodes by **category** — all nodes of the same type share one color. E.g. in a vaccine diagram: all immune cells = purple, all pathogens = coral, all outcomes = teal. - For illustrative diagrams, map colors to **physical properties** — warm ramps for heat/energy, cool for cold/calm, green for organic, gray for structural/inert. - Use **gray for neutral/structural** nodes (start, end, generic steps). - Use **2-3 colors per diagram**, not 6+. More colors = more visual noise. A diagram with gray + purple + teal is cleaner than one using every ramp. - **Prefer purple, teal, coral, pink** for general diagram categories. Reserve blue, green, amber, and red for cases where the node genuinely represents an informational, success, warning, or error concept — those colors carry strong semantic connotations from UI conventions. (Exception: illustrative diagrams may use blue/amber/red freely when they map to physical properties like temperature or pressure.) **Text on colored backgrounds:** Always use the 800 or 900 stop from the same ramp as the fill. Never use black, gray, or --color-text-primary on colored fills. **When a box has both a title and a subtitle, they must be two different stops** — title darker (800 in light mode, 100 in dark), subtitle lighter (600 in light, 200 in dark). Same stop for both reads flat; the weight difference alone isn't enough. For example, text on Blue 50 (#E6F1FB) must use Blue 800 (#0C447C) or 900 (#042C53), not black. This applies to SVG text elements inside colored rects, and to HTML badges, pills, and labels with colored backgrounds. **Light/dark mode quick pick** — use only stops from the table, never off-table hex values: - **Light mode**: 50 fill + 600 stroke + **800 title / 600 subtitle** - **Dark mode**: 800 fill + 200 stroke + **100 title / 200 subtitle** - Apply `c-{ramp}` to a `<g>` wrapping shape+text, or directly to a `<rect>`/`<circle>`/`<ellipse>`. Never to `<path>` — paths don't get ramp fill. For colored connector strokes use inline `stroke="#..."` (any mid-ramp hex works in both modes). Dark mode is automatic for ramp classes. Available: c-gray, c-blue, c-red, c-amber, c-green, c-teal, c-purple, c-coral, c-pink. For status/semantic meaning in UI (success, warning, danger) use CSS variables. For categorical coloring in both diagrams and UI, use these ramps. ## SVG setup **ViewBox safety checklist** — before finalizing any SVG, verify: 1. Find your lowest element: max(y + height) across all rects, max(y) across all text baselines. 2. Set viewBox height = that value + 40px buffer. 3. Find your rightmost element: max(x + width) across all rects. All content must stay within x=0 to x=680. 4. For text with text-anchor="end", the text extends LEFT from x. If x=118 and text is 200px wide, it starts at x=-82 — outside the viewBox. Increase x or use text-anchor="start". 5. Never use negative x or y coordinates. The viewBox starts at 0,0. 6. **No unintentional overlaps.** For every pair of elements that aren't meant to layer (label-on-label, label-on-arrow, box-on-box, callout-on-shape), check their bounding boxes do not intersect. The only allowed overlaps are deliberate: a label centered inside its own box, an arrowhead touching the box it points to, a highlight rect behind the thing it highlights. If two unrelated elements would collide, move one — shorten the label, shift the y, add a row. A diagram with crossed labels reads as broken regardless of how good the content is. 7. Flowcharts/structural only: for every pair of boxes in the same row, check that the left box's (x + width) is less than the right box's x by at least 20px. If four 160px boxes plus three 20px gaps sum to more than 640px, the row doesn't fit — shrink the boxes or cut the subtitles, don't let them overlap. **SVG setup**: `<svg width="100%" viewBox="0 0 680 H" role="img"><title>………` — 680px wide, flexible height. Here's how I'm thinking about the full stack and why each piece was chosen.

---

**The six layers and the rationale behind them**

The developer experience layer is just GitHub. Developers push to a repo; a GitHub Actions workflow builds the container, pushes it to GCP Artifact Registry, and updates a Kubernetes manifest in a central `platform` repo. That's the entire API surface a developer ever touches.

The control plane is where the magic happens. **Argo CD** watches the platform repo and reconciles whatever is declared there into the cluster — this is your GitOps engine. **KEDA** handles both autoscaling and hibernation: it can scale any workload to zero based on inactivity (no HTTP traffic for N hours → replica count 0, woken on next request by a KEDA HTTP add-on). **cert-manager** and **external-dns** automate all TLS and DNS record lifecycle.

The GKE runtime uses Kubernetes namespaces as your multi-tenancy primitive — one namespace per app, with `ResourceQuota` and `LimitRange` enforcing cost caps per app (and you can aggregate by owner label for per-user caps). This gives you strong isolation without exotic tooling.

Persistence is all managed GCP services, vended per-app at deploy time. No in-cluster databases to babysit.

The network layer is fully VPC-native and internal — apps can be made unreachable from the public internet simply by using an internal `Gateway`/`Ingress`. You still get valid HTTPS certificates and DNS records, just on a private zone.

Identity uses GitHub org membership as the source of truth. Workload Identity Federation lets your GitHub Actions pipelines authenticate to GCP without long-lived keys. App ownership is a label in the manifest —
Small revision, I as the designer/implementer and comfortable with k8s complexity but want to hide that from the operator of this PAAS. It is a key requirement to achieve low maintenance

That's an important distinction — it reshapes the design philosophy significantly.

The architecture stays the same underneath, but we need a **operator-facing abstraction layer** sitting above all that Kubernetes complexity. The operator should never need to write YAML, run `kubectl`, understand namespaces, or think about KEDA scalers. They should have a simple mental model:

> *"There are apps. Apps have owners. Apps have resources. Apps can be on or off."*

Let me think through what that abstraction looks like concretely:

This changes a few things concretely:

**The operator admin UI becomes a first-class deliverable**, not an afterthought. It's probably a small internal web app (could be as simple as a React frontend talking to a lightweight API that wraps `kubectl`/Argo CD calls). The operator never opens the GCP console or a terminal for routine tasks.

**The `paas.yaml` app manifest is the developer's entire configuration surface.** Something like:

```yaml
name: my-demo-app
owner: alice              # GitHub username
type: http                # http | worker | cronjob
schedule: "0 9 * * 1-5"  # if cronjob
tier: small               # small | medium | large → maps to ResourceQuota
private: true             # internal-only vs public ingress
persistence:
  database: postgres
  storage: true
  queue: true
```

That's it. No Kubernetes knowledge required from developers either.

**Low-maintenance for the operator means:**
- GitHub org sync is automatic — users appear/disappear without operator action
- Hibernation is automatic — apps that go quiet sleep themselves
- Cert renewal is automatic — cert-manager handles it
- The operator's routine work is: transfer ownership when someone leaves, occasionally adjust tiers or quotas, glance at the cost dashboard

**Two key open questions** before we start building:

1. **What does "operator" look like in practice?** Is this one named person with a dedicated admin role, or could it rotate? And do they need mobile-friendly access or is desktop-only fine?

2. **The admin UI** — do you want to build a custom one, or would you be comfortable with something like a lightly-configured Backstage, or even operator actions surfaced entirely through GitHub issues/PRs with a bot handling them?

The last option is interesting for low maintenance: the operator "manages" by commenting `/transfer-ownership @bob` on a GitHub issue and a bot does the Kubernetes work. No UI to build or host.

The key design consequences:

**`paas.yaml` ownership field changes** from a username to a team slug:
```yaml
owner: org/team-alpha   # was: owner: alice
```

**Deploy authorization** is now derived from team membership — any member of the owning team can push to that app's repos. This is checked at the GitHub Actions layer using the GitHub API, so there's no separate access control system to maintain.

**The operator's "transfer ownership" action** becomes: reassign an app's `owner` field from one team slug to another and commit it to the platform repo. Argo CD does the rest. The only case where the operator has to act is when a whole team dissolves — individual membership churn is now fully self-managing.

**Cost attribution** gets cleaner too — the admin UI can show a per-team spend rollup naturally, and quotas can be set at the team level (e.g. team-alpha gets max 10 apps, $150/mo cap).

**One new question this opens up:** when a developer registers a new app, they specify the owning team in `paas.yaml`. Should the PaaS validate at deploy time that the pusher is actually a member of that team (to prevent someone squatting another team's namespace), or do you trust the GitHub repo access model to handle that implicitly?

My instinct is yes — validate it — but it's worth calling out explicitly since it's a security boundary.

The security properties of this model are much stronger:

**What the OIDC token gives you for free.** GitHub's OIDC tokens are short-lived JWTs (5 min), signed by GitHub's key, and contain verifiable claims including the repo, the git ref, the workflow path, and — critically — the team(s) associated with the triggering actor. The PaaS verifies the signature against GitHub's public JWKS endpoint. No secret exchange needed, no token storage, no rotation burden.

**The blast radius if the PaaS is compromised** is now limited to what the PaaS itself can do — deploy apps, consume quota. It cannot enumerate your org, impersonate users, or read repo contents. That's a much tighter containment boundary.

**The remaining design question is the team model.** The OIDC token tells the PaaS "this deploy was triggered by a member of `org/team-alpha`" — but the PaaS still needs its own internal concept of a team to track app ownership, quotas, and cost attribution. The three options in the diagram represent a real tradeoff between operator control and friction for new teams.

My instinct is **Option C** (auto-create on first deploy, operator approves before quota is active) — it keeps onboarding frictionless for developers while giving the operator a meaningful gate before resources start being consumed. But this is exactly the kind of decision worth thinking through before we start building.

What's your read on that tradeoff?
Can we get the low maintenance of option A and the gating of option C  if we have default quotas that are applied to Apps without an explicit operator assigned quota?

Yes, exactly — and it's actually cleaner than Option C because there's no approval step to forget about or queue to drain.

The model becomes:

> **Every team gets in automatically. The default quota is just low enough that you can prove your app works, but not so generous that runaway costs are possible without operator awareness.**

The key insight is that **the default quota is the gate** — it just doesn't require any human to open it. The operator gets notified asynchronously rather than being in the critical path.

This also means the operator's workflow around teams becomes entirely reactive and low-pressure:

- New team appears → digest notification → glance at it → do nothing, or promote if you recognize the team as legitimate heavy users
- Team hits their default quota ceiling → they reach out → operator promotes them → takes 30 seconds in the admin UI
- Budget alert fires → operator reviews which teams are near their ceiling → adjusts as needed

**One design detail worth locking in:** what happens when a team hits their default quota and tries to deploy a 3rd app? The deploy should fail gracefully at the GitHub Actions layer with a clear error message — "team `org/team-alpha` has reached its app limit (2/2) on the default tier. Contact the platform operator to request a quota increase." That message does the work of routing the conversation to the right place without the operator needing to be involved upfront.

This feels like a solid model. Shall we start writing it down as a formal spec before moving into implementation? At this point we have enough design decisions to capture as a coherent document — it would be a useful artifact to refer back to as we build each layer iteratively.

content.text:
1	---
     2	name: docx
     3	description: "Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation."
     4	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     5	---
     6	
     7	# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis
     8	
     9	## Overview
    10	
    11	A .docx file is a ZIP archive containing XML files.
    12	
    13	## Quick Reference
    14	
    15	| Task | Approach |
    16	|------|----------|
    17	| Read/analyze content | `extract-text`, or unpack for raw XML |
    18	| Create new document | Use `docx-js` - see Creating New Documents below |
    19	| Edit existing document | Unpack → edit XML → repack - see Editing Existing Documents below |
    20	
    21	### Converting .doc to .docx
    22	
    23	Legacy `.doc` files must be converted before editing:
    24	
    25	```bash
    26	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx document.doc
    27	```
    28	
    29	### Reading Content
    30	
    31	```bash
    32	# Text extraction as markdown
    33	extract-text document.docx
    34	
    35	# Show tracked changes instead of accepting them
    36	pandoc --track-changes=all document.docx -o output.md
    37	
    38	# Raw XML access
    39	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
    40	```
    41	
    42	### Converting to Images
    43	
    44	```bash
    45	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf document.docx
    46	pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 document.pdf page
    47	```
    48	
    49	### Accepting Tracked Changes
    50	
    51	To produce a clean document with all tracked changes accepted (requires LibreOffice):
    52	
    53	```bash
    54	python scripts/accept_changes.py input.docx output.docx
    55	```
    56	
    57	---
    58	
    59	## Creating New Documents
    60	
    61	Generate .docx files with JavaScript, then validate. Install: `npm install -g docx`
    62	
    63	### Setup
    64	```javascript
    65	const { Document, Packer, Paragraph, TextRun, Table, TableRow, TableCell, ImageRun,
    66	        Header, Footer, AlignmentType, PageOrientation, LevelFormat, ExternalHyperlink,
    67	        InternalHyperlink, Bookmark, FootnoteReferenceRun, PositionalTab,
    68	        PositionalTabAlignment, PositionalTabRelativeTo, PositionalTabLeader,
    69	        TabStopType, TabStopPosition, Column, SectionType,
    70	        TableOfContents, HeadingLevel, BorderStyle, WidthType, ShadingType,
    71	        VerticalAlign, PageNumber, PageBreak } = require('docx');
    72	
    73	const doc = new Document({ sections: [{ children: [/* content */] }] });
    74	Packer.toBuffer(doc).then(buffer => fs.writeFileSync("doc.docx", buffer));
    75	```
    76	
    77	### Validation
    78	After creating the file, validate it. If validation fails, unpack, fix the XML, and repack.
    79	```bash
    80	python scripts/office/validate.py doc.docx
    81	```
    82	
    83	### Page Size
    84	
    85	```javascript
    86	// CRITICAL: docx-js defaults to A4, not US Letter
    87	// Always set page size explicitly for consistent results
    88	sections: [{
    89	  properties: {
    90	    page: {
    91	      size: {
    92	        width: 12240,   // 8.5 inches in DXA
    93	        height: 15840   // 11 inches in DXA
    94	      },
    95	      margin: { top: 1440, right: 1440, bottom: 1440, left: 1440 } // 1 inch margins
    96	    }
    97	  },
    98	  children: [/* content */]
    99	}]
   100	```
   101	
   102	**Common page sizes (DXA units, 1440 DXA = 1 inch):**
   103	
   104	| Paper | Width | Height | Content Width (1" margins) |
   105	|-------|-------|--------|---------------------------|
   106	| US Letter | 12,240 | 15,840 | 9,360 |
   107	| A4 (default) | 11,906 | 16,838 | 9,026 |
   108	
   109	**Landscape orientation:** docx-js swaps width/height internally, so pass portrait dimensions and let it handle the swap:
   110	```javascript
   111	size: {
   112	  width: 12240,   // Pass SHORT edge as width
   113	  height: 15840,  // Pass LONG edge as height
   114	  orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE  // docx-js swaps them in the XML
   115	},
   116	// Content width = 15840 - left margin - right margin (uses the long edge)
   117	```
   118	
   119	### Styles (Override Built-in Headings)
   120	
   121	Use Arial as the default font (universally supported). Keep titles black for readability.
   122	
   123	```javascript
   124	const doc = new Document({
   125	  styles: {
   126	    default: { document: { run: { font: "Arial", size: 24 } } }, // 12pt default
   127	    paragraphStyles: [
   128	      // IMPORTANT: Use exact IDs to override built-in styles
   129	      { id: "Heading1", name: "Heading 1", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   130	        run: { size: 32, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   131	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 240, after: 240 }, outlineLevel: 0 } }, // outlineLevel required for TOC
   132	      { id: "Heading2", name: "Heading 2", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   133	        run: { size: 28, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   134	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 180, after: 180 }, outlineLevel: 1 } },
   135	    ]
   136	  },
   137	  sections: [{
   138	    children: [
   139	      new Paragraph({ heading: HeadingLevel.HEADING_1, children: [new TextRun("Title")] }),
   140	    ]
   141	  }]
   142	});
   143	```
   144	
   145	### Lists (NEVER use unicode bullets)
   146	
   147	```javascript
   148	// ❌ WRONG - never manually insert bullet characters
   149	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("• Item")] })  // BAD
   150	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("\u2022 Item")] })  // BAD
   151	
   152	// ✅ CORRECT - use numbering config with LevelFormat.BULLET
   153	const doc = new Document({
   154	  numbering: {
   155	    config: [
   156	      { reference: "bullets",
   157	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.BULLET, text: "•", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   158	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   159	      { reference: "numbers",
   160	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.DECIMAL, text: "%1.", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   161	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   162	    ]
   163	  },
   164	  sections: [{
   165	    children: [
   166	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "bullets", level: 0 },
   167	        children: [new TextRun("Bullet item")] }),
   168	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "numbers", level: 0 },
   169	        children: [new TextRun("Numbered item")] }),
   170	    ]
   171	  }]
   172	});
   173	
   174	// ⚠️ Each reference creates INDEPENDENT numbering
   175	// Same reference = continues (1,2,3 then 4,5,6)
   176	// Different reference = restarts (1,2,3 then 1,2,3)
   177	```
   178	
   179	### Tables
   180	
   181	**CRITICAL: Tables need dual widths** - set both `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on each cell. Without both, tables render incorrectly on some platforms.
   182	
   183	```javascript
   184	// CRITICAL: Always set table width for consistent rendering
   185	// CRITICAL: Use ShadingType.CLEAR (not SOLID) to prevent black backgrounds
   186	const border = { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 1, color: "CCCCCC" };
   187	const borders = { top: border, bottom: border, left: border, right: border };
   188	
   189	new Table({
   190	  width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Always use DXA (percentages break in Google Docs)
   191	  columnWidths: [4680, 4680], // Must sum to table width (DXA: 1440 = 1 inch)
   192	  rows: [
   193	    new TableRow({
   194	      children: [
   195	        new TableCell({
   196	          borders,
   197	          width: { size: 4680, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Also set on each cell
   198	          shading: { fill: "D5E8F0", type: ShadingType.CLEAR }, // CLEAR not SOLID
   199	          margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }, // Cell padding (internal, not added to width)
   200	          children: [new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("Cell")] })]
   201	        })
   202	      ]
   203	    })
   204	  ]
   205	})
   206	```
   207	
   208	**Table width calculation:**
   209	
   210	Always use `WidthType.DXA` — `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` breaks in Google Docs.
   211	
   212	```javascript
   213	// Table width = sum of columnWidths = content width
   214	// US Letter with 1" margins: 12240 - 2880 = 9360 DXA
   215	width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA },
	< truncated lines 216-378 >
   379	```
   380	
   381	### Critical Rules for docx-js
   382	
   383	- **Set page size explicitly** - docx-js defaults to A4; use US Letter (12240 x 15840 DXA) for US documents
   384	- **Landscape: pass portrait dimensions** - docx-js swaps width/height internally; pass short edge as `width`, long edge as `height`, and set `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE`
   385	- **Never use `\n`** - use separate Paragraph elements
   386	- **Never use unicode bullets** - use `LevelFormat.BULLET` with numbering config
   387	- **PageBreak must be in Paragraph** - standalone creates invalid XML
   388	- **ImageRun requires `type`** - always specify png/jpg/etc
   389	- **Always set table `width` with DXA** - never use `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` (breaks in Google Docs)
   390	- **Tables need dual widths** - `columnWidths` array AND cell `width`, both must match
   391	- **Table width = sum of columnWidths** - for DXA, ensure they add up exactly
   392	- **Always add cell margins** - use `margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }` for readable padding
   393	- **Use `ShadingType.CLEAR`** - never SOLID for table shading
   394	- **Never use tables as dividers/rules** - cells have minimum height and render as empty boxes (including in headers/footers); use `border: { bottom: { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 6, color: "2E75B6", space: 1 } }` on a Paragraph instead. For two-column footers, use tab stops (see Tab Stops section), not tables
   395	- **TOC requires HeadingLevel only** - no custom styles on heading paragraphs
   396	- **Override built-in styles** - use exact IDs: "Heading1", "Heading2", etc.
   397	- **Include `outlineLevel`** - required for TOC (0 for H1, 1 for H2, etc.)
   398	
   399	---
   400	
   401	## Editing Existing Documents
   402	
   403	**Follow all 3 steps in order.**
   404	
   405	### Step 1: Unpack
   406	```bash
   407	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
   408	```
   409	Extracts XML, pretty-prints, merges adjacent runs, and converts smart quotes to XML entities (`“` etc.) so they survive editing. Use `--merge-runs false` to skip run merging.
   410	
   411	### Step 2: Edit XML
   412	
   413	Edit files in `unpacked/word/`. See XML Reference below for patterns.
   414	
   415	**Use "Claude" as the author** for tracked changes and comments, unless the user explicitly requests use of a different name.
   416	
   417	**Use the Edit tool directly for string replacement. Do not write Python scripts.** Scripts introduce unnecessary complexity. The Edit tool shows exactly what is being replaced.
   418	
   419	**CRITICAL: Use smart quotes for new content.** When adding text with apostrophes or quotes, use XML entities to produce smart quotes:
   420	```xml
   421	<!-- Use these entities for professional typography -->
   422	<w:t>Here’s a quote: “Hello”</w:t>
   423	```
   424	| Entity | Character |
   425	|--------|-----------|
   426	| `‘` | ‘ (left single) |
   427	| `’` | ’ (right single / apostrophe) |
   428	| `“` | “ (left double) |
   429	| `”` | ” (right double) |
   430	
   431	**Adding comments:** Use `comment.py` to handle boilerplate across multiple XML files (text must be pre-escaped XML):
   432	```bash
   433	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Comment text with & and ’"
   434	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 1 "Reply text" --parent 0  # reply to comment 0
   435	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Text" --author "Custom Author"  # custom author name
   436	```
   437	Then add markers to document.xml (see Comments in XML Reference).
   438	
   439	### Step 3: Pack
   440	```bash
   441	python scripts/office/pack.py unpacked/ output.docx --original document.docx
   442	```
   443	Validates with auto-repair, condenses XML, and creates DOCX. Use `--validate false` to skip.
   444	
   445	**Auto-repair will fix:**
   446	- `durableId` >= 0x7FFFFFFF (regenerates valid ID)
   447	- Missing `xml:space="preserve"` on `<w:t>` with whitespace
   448	
   449	**Auto-repair won't fix:**
   450	- Malformed XML, invalid element nesting, missing relationships, schema violations
   451	
   452	### Common Pitfalls
   453	
   454	- **Replace entire `<w:r>` elements**: When adding tracked changes, replace the whole `<w:r>...</w:r>` block with `<w:del>...<w:ins>...` as siblings. Don't inject tracked change tags inside a run.
   455	- **Preserve `<w:rPr>` formatting**: Copy the original run's `<w:rPr>` block into your tracked change runs to maintain bold, font size, etc.
   456	
   457	---
   458	
   459	## XML Reference
   460	
   461	### Schema Compliance
   462	
   463	- **Element order in `<w:pPr>`**: `<w:pStyle>`, `<w:numPr>`, `<w:spacing>`, `<w:ind>`, `<w:jc>`, `<w:rPr>` last
   464	- **Whitespace**: Add `xml:space="preserve"` to `<w:t>` with leading/trailing spaces
   465	- **RSIDs**: Must be 8-digit hex (e.g., `00AB1234`)
   466	
   467	### Tracked Changes
   468	
   469	**Insertion:**
   470	```xml
   471	<w:ins w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   472	  <w:r><w:t>inserted text</w:t></w:r>
   473	</w:ins>
   474	```
   475	
   476	**Deletion:**
   477	```xml
   478	<w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   479	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   480	</w:del>
   481	```
   482	
   483	**Inside `<w:del>`**: Use `<w:delText>` instead of `<w:t>`, and `<w:delInstrText>` instead of `<w:instrText>`.
   484	
   485	**Minimal edits** - only mark what changes:
   486	```xml
   487	<!-- Change "30 days" to "60 days" -->
   488	<w:r><w:t>The term is </w:t></w:r>
   489	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   490	  <w:r><w:delText>30</w:delText></w:r>
   491	</w:del>
   492	<w:ins w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   493	  <w:r><w:t>60</w:t></w:r>
   494	</w:ins>
   495	<w:r><w:t> days.</w:t></w:r>
   496	```
   497	
   498	**Deleting entire paragraphs/list items** - when removing ALL content from a paragraph, also mark the paragraph mark as deleted so it merges with the next paragraph. Add `<w:del/>` inside `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`:
   499	```xml
   500	<w:p>
   501	  <w:pPr>
   502	    <w:numPr>...</w:numPr>  <!-- list numbering if present -->
   503	    <w:rPr>
   504	      <w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"/>
   505	    </w:rPr>
   506	  </w:pPr>
   507	  <w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   508	    <w:r><w:delText>Entire paragraph content being deleted...</w:delText></w:r>
   509	  </w:del>
   510	</w:p>
   511	```
   512	Without the `<w:del/>` in `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`, accepting changes leaves an empty paragraph/list item.
   513	
   514	**Rejecting another author's insertion** - nest deletion inside their insertion:
   515	```xml
   516	<w:ins w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   517	  <w:del w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   518	    <w:r><w:delText>their inserted text</w:delText></w:r>
   519	  </w:del>
   520	</w:ins>
   521	```
   522	
   523	**Restoring another author's deletion** - add insertion after (don't modify their deletion):
   524	```xml
   525	<w:del w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   526	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   527	</w:del>
   528	<w:ins w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   529	  <w:r><w:t>deleted text</w:t></w:r>
   530	</w:ins>
   531	```
   532	
   533	### Comments
   534	
   535	After running `comment.py` (see Step 2), add markers to document.xml. For replies, use `--parent` flag and nest markers inside the parent's.
   536	
   537	**CRITICAL: `<w:commentRangeStart>` and `<w:commentRangeEnd>` are siblings of `<w:r>`, never inside `<w:r>`.**
   538	
   539	```xml
   540	<!-- Comment markers are direct children of w:p, never inside w:r -->
   541	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   542	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   543	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted</w:delText></w:r>
   544	</w:del>
   545	<w:r><w:t> more text</w:t></w:r>
   546	<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
   547	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
   548	
   549	<!-- Comment 0 with reply 1 nested inside -->
   550	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   551	  <w:commentRangeStart w:id="1"/>
   552	  <w:r><w:t>text</w:t></w:r>
   553	  <w:commentRangeEnd w:id="1"/>
   554	<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
   555	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
   556	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="1"/></w:r>
   557	```
   558	
   559	### Images
   560	
   561	1. Add image file to `word/media/`
   562	2. Add relationship to `word/_rels/document.xml.rels`:
   563	```xml
   564	<Relationship Id="rId5" Type=".../image" Target="media/image1.png"/>
   565	```
   566	3. Add content type to `[Content_Types].xml`:
   567	```xml
   568	<Default Extension="png" ContentType="image/png"/>
   569	```
   570	4. Reference in document.xml:
   571	```xml
   572	<w:drawing>
   573	  <wp:inline>
   574	    <wp:extent cx="914400" cy="914400"/>  <!-- EMUs: 914400 = 1 inch -->
   575	    <a:graphic>
   576	      <a:graphicData uri=".../picture">
   577	        <pic:pic>
   578	          <pic:blipFill><a:blip r:embed="rId5"/></pic:blipFill>
   579	        </pic:pic>
   580	      </a:graphicData>
   581	    </a:graphic>
   582	  </wp:inline>
   583	</w:drawing>
   584	```
   585	
   586	---
   587	
   588	## Dependencies
   589	
   590	- **pandoc**: Text extraction
   591	- **docx**: `npm install -g docx` (new documents)
   592	- **LibreOffice**: PDF conversion (auto-configured for sandboxed environments via `scripts/office/soffice.py`)
   593	- **Poppler**: `pdftoppm` for images
   594

# Non-Production PaaS — Design & Architecture Specification

> **Version:** 0.1 · **Status:** Draft · **Date:** May 2026

A self-hosted platform-as-a-service for hosting non-production applications (demos, experiments) in a dedicated GCP project. Designed for low operator maintenance with strong cost controls and a Heroku-style developer experience.

---

## Table of contents

1. [Goals and non-goals](#1-goals-and-non-goals)
2. [Personas](#2-personas)
3. [Architecture overview](#3-architecture-overview)
4. [Security model](#4-security-model)
5. [Ownership model](#5-ownership-model)
6. [Team and quota model](#6-team-and-quota-model)
7. [Developer interface](#7-developer-interface)
8. [Operator interface](#8-operator-interface)
9. [Hibernation](#9-hibernation)
10. [Key decisions log](#10-key-decisions-log)
11. [Open questions](#11-open-questions)
12. [Iterative build plan](#12-iterative-build-plan)

---

## 1. Goals and non-goals

### Goals

- Let developers deploy containerised apps with nothing more than a git push
- Support HTTP servers, background workers, and scheduled jobs
- Provide managed persistence: blob storage, databases, and queues
- Enforce cost caps automatically; require no manual intervention for routine use
- Detect and hibernate idle apps; wake them transparently on next request
- Manage DNS and HTTPS automatically under an operator-controlled domain
- Keep apps unreachable from the public internet when required
- Allow ownership transfer of apps between teams without downtime
- Require part-time attention from a single, rotating operator

### Non-goals

- Production workloads — this platform has no SLA
- Multi-region or high-availability deployments
- Workloads requiring GPUs or specialised hardware
- Replacing an internal developer portal (Backstage, etc.)
- Serving as a general-purpose CI/CD platform

---

## 2. Personas

### Designer / implementer

Builds and evolves the platform itself. Comfortable with Kubernetes internals, Terraform, Helm, and GCP. Interacts with the full stack. This role is not the operator; complexity is acceptable here because it is absorbed once during construction and rarely during maintenance.

### Operator

Manages the running platform on a part-time basis. The role may rotate. The operator has no expectation of Kubernetes or GCP knowledge. Their entire workflow is through a purpose-built admin UI. Routine tasks should take minutes, not hours.

The operator's task surface is deliberately narrow:

- Review new teams that have auto-registered
- Promote teams to higher quota tiers on request
- Transfer app ownership when a team is dissolved
- Glance at cost and health dashboards
- Act on alerts (failed deploys, budget thresholds, expiring certs)

### Developer / app owner

A member of the GitHub organisation. Deploys and operates apps on behalf of their team. No cloud or Kubernetes knowledge required. Their entire interface is a git repository and a `paas.yaml` manifest in its root.

---

## 3. Architecture overview

The platform is built on GKE running in a dedicated non-production GCP project. Kubernetes complexity is fully hidden from operators and developers; only the designer interacts with it directly.

| Layer | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Developer experience | `git push` triggers GitHub Actions: build container, push to Artifact Registry, call PaaS deploy API |
| Control plane | Argo CD (GitOps), KEDA (autoscaling + hibernation), cert-manager, external-dns |
| GKE runtime | One namespace per app; Deployments, CronJobs, ResourceQuotas, LimitRanges |
| Persistence | GCS buckets, Cloud SQL, Cloud Pub/Sub — managed, one resource per app |
| Network / DNS / TLS | GKE Gateway API, VPC-native, internal load balancer, Cloud DNS, Let's Encrypt |
| Identity / cost | GitHub OIDC tokens, Workload Identity Federation, GCP budget alerts, Namespace ResourceQuota |

---

## 4. Security model

### Core principle: GitHub calls the PaaS, not the other way around

An earlier design considered the PaaS polling the GitHub API to sync team membership. This was rejected because it required the PaaS to hold a long-lived GitHub token with org-level read access — a token that, if leaked, could enumerate all org members, teams, and repositories.

The adopted model inverts the relationship: GitHub Actions calls the PaaS API and presents a short-lived OIDC token as proof of identity. The PaaS never holds a GitHub credential of any kind.

### GitHub OIDC token flow

1. GitHub Actions generates a short-lived JWT (5-minute TTL) signed by GitHub's private key
2. The token contains verifiable claims: repository, git ref, workflow SHA, and the triggering actor's team membership
3. The PaaS validates the token signature against GitHub's public JWKS endpoint (read-only, no credential required)
4. The PaaS extracts the team claim and uses it for authorisation

### What the PaaS holds vs. never holds

| PaaS holds | PaaS never holds |
|---|---|
| GitHub's public JWKS URL (read-only) | GitHub PAT or OAuth token |
| Its own internal team and app records | Org membership read access |
| GCP service account credentials (via Workload Identity) | Any credential that can enumerate the GitHub org |

### Blast radius if the PaaS is compromised

An attacker who fully compromises the PaaS can: deploy or delete apps on the platform, exhaust quota, and access data in platform-managed persistence.

They cannot: enumerate the GitHub organisation, read source code, impersonate users outside the platform, or access other GCP projects.

---

## 5. Ownership model

### GitHub teams as owners

Apps are owned by GitHub teams, not individual users. This makes ownership stable across membership churn: when someone joins or leaves a team, access follows automatically without any operator action.

The `owner` field in `paas.yaml` is a team slug in the form `org/team-name`.

### Membership lifecycle

| Event | Platform behaviour |
|---|---|
| Member joins a team | Automatically gains deploy access to that team's apps on next deploy. No operator action. |
| Member leaves the org | Access revoked on next OIDC token validation. Apps remain under team ownership. |
| Team dissolved | Operator transfers app ownership to another team via the admin UI. Only case requiring operator action. |

---

## 6. Team and quota model

### Automatic team onboarding

When the PaaS receives the first deploy request from a previously unknown GitHub team, it automatically creates a team record and assigns the default quota tier. The deploy succeeds immediately. The operator receives a digest notification but is not in the critical path.

This achieves low-maintenance onboarding while bounding cost exposure through the default tier limits.

### Quota tiers

| Attribute | Default tier | Standard tier | Power tier | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Assignment | Automatic | Operator assigned | Operator assigned | Default on first deploy |
| Max apps | 2 | 10 | 25 | Per team |
| CPU per app | 0.5 cores | 1 core | 4 cores | Kubernetes limit |
| Memory per app | 512 MB | 1 GB | 4 GB | Kubernetes limit |
| Storage | 10 GB | 100 GB | 500 GB | GCS + Cloud SQL combined |
| Max cost exposure | ~$15/mo | ~$80/mo | ~$300/mo | Estimated ceiling |
| Hibernate after | 24 hrs idle | 48 hrs idle | 72 hrs idle | Configurable per app |

The default tier is intentionally sized so that a team can validate a working application without hitting constraints, but cannot consume meaningful budget without the operator becoming aware.

### Quota enforcement

- Kubernetes `ResourceQuota` and `LimitRange` enforce CPU and memory at the namespace level
- When a team hits their app count limit, the deploy API returns a clear error directing them to contact the operator
- Budget alerts fire at 80% and 100% of tier ceiling; operator is notified but no automatic action is taken
- Operator can promote a team's tier in the admin UI in under 30 seconds

---

## 7. Developer interface

### paas.yaml

The entire configuration surface for a developer is a `paas.yaml` in the root of their repository. No Kubernetes knowledge required.

```yaml
name: my-demo-app
owner: org/team-alpha        # GitHub team slug
type: http                   # http | worker | cronjob
schedule: "0 9 * * 1-5"     # required if type: cronjob
tier: small                  # small | medium | large (within team quota)
private: true                # internal-only ingress if true
persistence:
  database: postgres         # omit if not needed
  storage: true
  queue: true
```

### Deploy flow

1. Developer pushes to the default branch
2. GitHub Actions: lint, test, build container, push to Artifact Registry
3. Workflow calls the PaaS deploy API with the new image digest and OIDC token
4. PaaS validates token, checks team ownership and quota, updates the app's manifest
5. Argo CD detects the manifest change and reconciles cluster state
6. App is live within seconds of Argo CD sync

---

## 8. Operator interface

The operator interacts exclusively with a purpose-built web admin UI (desktop). No terminal, kubectl, or GCP console access is required for routine operations.

### Admin UI task surface

| Area | Actions |
|---|---|
| App management | View all apps with owner, status, cost; hibernate/wake/delete; transfer ownership; adjust resource tier |
| Team management | View all teams; per-team app count and cost; promote/demote quota tier; suspend a team |
| Cost and quotas | Total and per-team spend; budget alert thresholds; apps approaching quota ceiling; hibernate candidates |
| Platform health | Cluster status summary; failed deploy log; cert and DNS alerts; upgrade notifications |

### Routine operator cadence

Expected time investment is a few hours per month. No operator action is required for normal day-to-day developer activity.

- **Weekly:** glance at cost dashboard and new team digest
- **On request:** promote a team's quota tier when they hit their limit
- **On offboarding:** transfer app ownership when a team is dissolved
- **On alert:** investigate cert, DNS, or budget alerts

---

## 9. Hibernation

Apps that receive no traffic for their configured idle threshold are automatically scaled to zero replicas by KEDA. Persistence is retained. The app wakes transparently on the next HTTP request via the KEDA HTTP add-on, which holds the request while the pod starts.

| Property | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Idle detection | KEDA monitors HTTP request rate; zero requests for idle threshold triggers scale-to-zero |
| Wake-on-request | KEDA HTTP add-on holds the first request while the pod initialises |
| Cold start time | Typically 5–15 seconds depending on container image size |
| Persistence during hibernation | All data retained; no cleanup of database or storage |
| Worker hibernation | Workers scale to zero when their queue is empty (KEDA queue scaler) |
| CronJob hibernation | CronJobs suspended when app is hibernated; schedule resumes on wake |

---

## 10. Key decisions log

| Requirement | Decision | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Infrastructure | GKE (full Kubernetes control plane) | Scale target (50+ users, 500+ apps) rules out simpler managed options. Designer is comfortable with K8s complexity. |
| GitOps engine | Argo CD | Mature, well-supported, integrates cleanly with Kubernetes manifests. Pull-based model keeps cluster as source of truth. |
| Autoscale / hibernate | KEDA + KEDA HTTP add-on | Single tool handles queue-driven worker scaling and HTTP-driven hibernation. Scale-to-zero is native. |
| GitHub integration | Push model (GitHub calls PaaS) | Pull model requires long-lived GitHub token with org-read scope. Rejected on security grounds. OIDC tokens are short-lived and carry no org-level access. |
| App ownership | GitHub teams (not individuals) | Teams are stable across membership churn. Individual ownership requires operator action on every departure. |
| Team onboarding | Automatic with default quota | Manual onboarding is high operator burden. Automatic onboarding with a low default quota bounds cost exposure without blocking developers. |
| Quota tiers | Three tiers: default, standard, power | Coarse tiers are easier to explain and administer than per-app limits. Default auto-assigned; upper tiers require operator action. |
| Operator tooling | Custom admin UI (web, desktop) | Operator may rotate and has no K8s/GCP knowledge. kubectl and GCP console are not acceptable operator interfaces. |
| Persistence | GCS, Cloud SQL, Cloud Pub/Sub | Fully managed GCP services; no in-cluster databases to operate. One resource per app for isolation. |
| DNS / TLS | external-dns + cert-manager + Let's Encrypt | Fully automated; zero operator involvement in cert renewal or DNS record management. |

---

## 11. Open questions

These should be resolved before implementation of the relevant phase begins.

- What is the operator's notification channel? (Slack, email, or both?)
- What domain will the platform manage? (e.g. `apps.internal.example.com`)
- Should the idle threshold be configurable per-app in `paas.yaml`, or set platform-wide by the operator?
- How should database credentials be vended to apps? (Kubernetes Secrets, GCP Secret Manager, or both?)
- What is the GCP project naming convention and overall budget ceiling?
- Should the admin UI authenticate via GitHub OAuth (tying operator identity to org membership), or use a standalone credential?
- What is the process for the designer to push platform upgrades (GKE versions, Helm chart updates) with minimal operator disruption?

---

## 12. Iterative build plan

The platform is built incrementally. Each phase is independently useful and testable before the next begins.

| Phase | Scope |
|---|---|
| 1 — Foundation | GCP project, GKE cluster, Artifact Registry, VPC, Terraform baseline |
| 2 — GitOps core | Argo CD, namespace-per-app scaffolding, basic `paas.yaml` manifest rendering |
| 3 — Deploy API | PaaS API service, GitHub OIDC validation, team auto-registration, quota enforcement |
| 4 — Networking | GKE Gateway API, internal/external ingress, cert-manager, external-dns, custom domain |
| 5 — Persistence | GCS bucket provisioning, Cloud SQL vending, Pub/Sub topic creation, secret injection |
| 6 — Hibernation | KEDA, HTTP add-on, idle detection, scale-to-zero, wake-on-request |
| 7 — Admin UI | Operator web UI: app list, team management, quota promotion, cost dashboard |
| 8 — Hardening | Budget alerts, audit logging, disaster recovery runbook, operator handover docs |

Each phase will produce a working, reviewable increment. Design decisions specific to a phase will be captured as addenda to this document before that phase begins.

The registry needs to be private, and there are two distinct credential problems to solve:

**At pull time (GKE → Artifact Registry):** also clean — GKE nodes authenticate to Artifact Registry using the node pool's GCP service account, which is granted `roles/artifactregistry.reader` on the registry. No credentials involved at all; it's ambient GCP identity.

**The one wrinkle worth calling out explicitly:** the Artifact Registry should be in the same GCP project as the cluster (or a dedicated images project if you later want to share images across projects). Cross-project pulls work but require explicit IAM grants that are easy to miss.

One additional consideration — should each team's images be isolated within the registry (separate repositories per team), or is a single flat repository acceptable? 1. [Goals and non-goals](#1-goals-and-non-goals)
2. [Personas](#2-personas)
3. [Architecture overview](#3-architecture-overview)
4. [Security model](#4-security-model)
5. [Ownership model](#5-ownership-model)
6. [Team and quota model](#6-team-and-quota-model)
7. [Developer interface](#7-developer-interface)
8. [Operator interface](#8-operator-interface)
9. [Hibernation](#9-hibernation)
10. [Key decisions log](#10-key-decisions-log)
11. [Open questions](#11-open-questions)

### Goals

- Let developers deploy containerised apps with nothing more than a git push
- Support HTTP servers, background workers, and scheduled jobs

- Enforce cost caps automatically; require no manual intervention for routine use
- Detect and hibernate idle apps; wake them transparently on next request
- Manage DNS and HTTPS automatically under an operator-controlled domain
- Keep apps unreachable from the public internet when required
- Allow ownership transfer of apps between teams without downtime
- Require part-time attention from a single, rotating operator

### Non-goals

- Production workloads — this platform has no SLA
- Multi-region or high-availability deployments
- Workloads requiring GPUs or specialised hardware
- Replacing an internal developer portal (Backstage, etc.)
- Serving as a general-purpose CI/CD platform

### Designer / implementer

Builds and evolves the platform itself. Comfortable with Kubernetes internals, Terraform, Helm, and GCP. Interacts with the full stack. This role is not the operator; complexity is acceptable here because it is absorbed once during construction and rarely during maintenance.

| Layer | Responsibility |

1. GitHub Actions generates a short-lived JWT (5-minute TTL) signed by GitHub's private key
2. The token contains verifiable claims: repository, git ref, workflow SHA, and the triggering actor's team membership
3. The PaaS validates the token signature against GitHub's public JWKS endpoint (read-only, no credential required)
4. The PaaS extracts the team claim and uses it for authorisation

| PaaS holds | PaaS never holds |
|---|---|
| GitHub's public JWKS URL (read-only) | GitHub PAT or OAuth token |
| Its own internal team and app records | Org membership read access |
| GCP service account credentials (via Workload Identity) | Any credential that can enumerate the GitHub org |

|---|---|

| Hibernate after | 24 hrs idle | 48 hrs idle | 72 hrs idle | Configurable per app |

- Kubernetes `ResourceQuota` and `LimitRange` enforce CPU and memory at the namespace level

| Area | Actions |
|---|---|
| App management | View all apps with owner, status, cost; hibernate/wake/delete; transfer ownership; adjust resource tier |

- **On request:** promote a team's quota tier when they hit their limit
- **On offboarding:** transfer app ownership when a team is dissolved
- **On alert:** investigate cert, DNS, or budget alerts

- Should the idle threshold be configurable per-app in `paas.yaml`, or set platform-wide by the operator?

# Morsel — Design & Architecture Specification

> **Version:** 0.1 · **Status:** Draft · **Date:** May 2026

A self-hosted platform-as-a-service for hosting non-production applications (demos, experiments) in a dedicated GCP project. Designed for low operator maintenance with strong cost controls and a Heroku-style developer experience.

---

## Table of contents

1. [Goals and non-goals](#1-goals-and-non-goals)
2. [Personas](#2-personas)
3. [Architecture overview](#3-architecture-overview)
4. [Security model](#4-security-model)
5. [Ownership model](#5-ownership-model)
6. [Team and quota model](#6-team-and-quota-model)
7. [Developer interface](#7-developer-interface)
8. [Operator interface](#8-operator-interface)
9. [Hibernation](#9-hibernation)
10. [Key decisions log](#10-key-decisions-log)
11. [Open questions](#11-open-questions)
12. [Iterative build plan](#12-iterative-build-plan)

---

## 1. Goals and non-goals

### Goals

- Let developers deploy containerised apps with nothing more than a git push
- Support HTTP servers, background workers, and scheduled jobs
- Provide managed persistence: blob storage, databases, and queues
- Enforce cost caps automatically; require no manual intervention for routine use
- Detect and hibernate idle apps; wake them transparently on next request
- Manage DNS and HTTPS automatically under an operator-controlled domain
- Keep apps unreachable from the public internet when required
- Allow ownership transfer of apps between teams without downtime
- Require part-time attention from a single, rotating operator

### Non-goals

- Production workloads — Morsel has no SLA
- Multi-region or high-availability deployments
- Workloads requiring GPUs or specialised hardware
- Replacing an internal developer portal (Backstage, etc.)
- Serving as a general-purpose CI/CD platform

---

## 2. Personas

### Designer / implementer

Builds and evolves the platform itself. Comfortable with Kubernetes internals, Terraform, Helm, and GCP. Interacts with the full stack. This role is not the operator; complexity is acceptable here because it is absorbed once during construction and rarely during maintenance.

### Operator

Manages the running platform on a part-time basis. The role may rotate. The operator has no expectation of Kubernetes or GCP knowledge. Their entire workflow is through a purpose-built admin UI. Routine tasks should take minutes, not hours.

The operator's task surface is deliberately narrow:

- Review new teams that have auto-registered
- Promote teams to higher quota tiers on request
- Transfer app ownership when a team is dissolved
- Glance at cost and health dashboards
- Act on alerts (failed deploys, budget thresholds, expiring certs)

### Developer / app owner

A member of the GitHub organisation. Deploys and operates apps on behalf of their team. No cloud or Kubernetes knowledge required. Their entire interface is a git repository and a `morsel.json` manifest in its root.

---

## 3. Architecture overview

Morsel is built on GKE running in a dedicated non-production GCP project. Kubernetes complexity is fully hidden from operators and developers; only the designer interacts with it directly.

| Layer | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Developer experience | `git push` triggers GitHub Actions: build container, push to Artifact Registry, call Morsel deploy API |
| Control plane | Argo CD (GitOps), KEDA (autoscaling + hibernation), cert-manager, external-dns |
| GKE runtime | One namespace per app; Deployments, CronJobs, ResourceQuotas, LimitRanges |
| Persistence | GCS buckets, Cloud SQL, Cloud Pub/Sub — managed, one resource per app |
| Network / DNS / TLS | GKE Gateway API, VPC-native, internal load balancer, Cloud DNS, Let's Encrypt |
| Identity / cost | GitHub OIDC tokens, Workload Identity Federation, GCP budget alerts, Namespace ResourceQuota |

---

## 4. Security model

### Core principle: GitHub calls Morsel, not the other way around

GitHub Actions calls the Morsel API and presents a short-lived OIDC token as proof of identity. Morsel never holds a GitHub credential of any kind.

### GitHub OIDC token flow

1. GitHub Actions generates a short-lived JWT (5-minute TTL) signed by GitHub's private key
2. The token contains verifiable claims: repository, git ref, workflow SHA, and the triggering actor's team membership
3. Morsel validates the token signature against GitHub's public JWKS endpoint (read-only, no credential required)
4. Morsel extracts the team claim and uses it for authorisation

### What Morsel holds vs. never holds

| Morsel holds | Morsel never holds |
|---|---|
| GitHub's public JWKS URL (read-only) | GitHub PAT or OAuth token |
| Its own internal team and app records | Org membership read access |
| GCP service account credentials (via Workload Identity) | Any credential that can enumerate the GitHub org |

### Blast radius if Morsel is compromised

An attacker who fully compromises Morsel can: deploy or delete apps on the platform, exhaust quota, and access data in platform-managed persistence.

They cannot: enumerate the GitHub organisation, read source code, impersonate users outside the platform, or access other GCP projects.

### Artifact Registry access

Container images are stored in a private GCP Artifact Registry. Access is credential-free in both directions.

**Push (GitHub Actions → Artifact Registry):** Workload Identity Federation allows GitHub Actions to authenticate to GCP using the same OIDC token presented to the Morsel API. No long-lived credentials are stored in GitHub.

**Pull (GKE → Artifact Registry):** GKE node pools authenticate using their attached GCP service account, which is granted `roles/artifactregistry.reader` on the registry. No credentials are required at the pod or namespace level.

**Registry structure:** Each team gets a dedicated repository within the registry (e.g. `REGION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/team-alpha/app-name`). Separate repositories scope push permissions so that a team can only write to their own images. Cross-team overwrites are not possible. The Morsel deploy API enforces that the image digest presented in a deploy request originates from the calling team's repository.

**Registry location:** The Artifact Registry lives in the same GCP project as the GKE cluster. Cross-project image pulls are avoided to keep IAM configuration simple and reduce latency.

---

## 5. Ownership model

### GitHub teams as owners

Apps are owned by GitHub teams, not individual users. This makes ownership stable across membership churn: when someone joins or leaves a team, access follows automatically without any operator action.

The `owner` field in `morsel.json` is a team slug in the form `org/team-name`.

### Membership lifecycle

| Event | Platform behaviour |
|---|---|
| Member joins a team | Automatically gains deploy access to that team's apps on next deploy. No operator action. |
| Member leaves the org | Access revoked on next OIDC token validation. Apps remain under team ownership. |
| Team dissolved | Operator transfers app ownership to another team via the admin UI. Only case requiring operator action. |

---

## 6. Team and quota model

### Automatic team onboarding

When Morsel receives the first deploy request from a previously unknown GitHub team, it automatically creates a team record and assigns the default quota tier. The deploy succeeds immediately. The operator receives a digest notification but is not in the critical path.

This achieves low-maintenance onboarding while bounding cost exposure through the default tier limits.

### Quota tiers

| Attribute | Default tier | Standard tier | Power tier | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Assignment | Automatic | Operator assigned | Operator assigned | Default on first deploy |
| Max apps | 2 | 10 | 25 | Per team |
| CPU per app | 0.5 cores | 1 core | 4 cores | Kubernetes limit |
| Memory per app | 512 MB | 1 GB | 4 GB | Kubernetes limit |
| Storage | 10 GB | 100 GB | 500 GB | GCS + Cloud SQL combined |
| Max cost exposure | ~$15/mo | ~$80/mo | ~$300/mo | Estimated ceiling |
| Hibernate after | 24 hrs idle | 48 hrs idle | 72 hrs idle | Configurable per app |

The default tier is intentionally sized so that a team can validate a working application without hitting constraints, but cannot consume meaningful budget without the operator becoming aware.

### Quota enforcement

- Kubernetes `ResourceQuota` and `LimitRange` enforce CPU and memory at the namespace level
- When a team hits their app count limit, the deploy API returns a clear error directing them to contact the operator
- Budget alerts fire at 80% and 100% of tier ceiling; operator is notified but no automatic action is taken
- Operator can promote a team's tier in the admin UI in under 30 seconds

---

## 7. Developer interface

### morsel.json

The entire configuration surface for a developer is a `morsel.json` in the root of their repository. No Kubernetes knowledge required.

```json
{
  "name": "my-demo-app",
  "owner": "org/team-alpha",
  "type": "http",
  "schedule": "0 9 * * 1-5",
  "tier": "small",
  "private": true,
  "persistence": {
    "database": "postgres",
    "storage": true,
    "queue": true
  }
}
```

| Field | Values | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | Unique within the team. Becomes the subdomain. |
| `owner` | `org/team-name` | GitHub team slug. Must match the OIDC token claim. |
| `type` | `http` \| `worker` \| `cronjob` | Determines the Kubernetes workload type. |
| `schedule` | cron expression | Required when `type` is `cronjob`. |
| `tier` | `small` \| `medium` \| `large` | Resource size within the team's quota tier. |
| `private` | boolean | `true` for internal-only ingress; `false` for public. |
| `persistence.database` | `postgres` \| `mysql` | Provisions a Cloud SQL instance. Omit if not needed. |
| `persistence.storage` | boolean | Provisions a GCS bucket. |
| `persistence.queue` | boolean | Provisions a Pub/Sub topic and subscription. |

### Deploy flow

1. Developer pushes to the default branch
2. GitHub Actions: lint, test, build container, push to team's Artifact Registry repository
3. Workflow calls the Morsel deploy API with the new image digest and OIDC token
4. Morsel validates the token, verifies the image originates from the team's registry repository, checks ownership and quota, updates the app's manifest
5. Argo CD detects the manifest change and reconciles cluster state
6. App is live within seconds of Argo CD sync

---

## 8. Operator interface

The operator interacts exclusively with a purpose-built web admin UI (desktop). No terminal, kubectl, or GCP console access is required for routine operations.

### Admin UI task surface

| Area | Actions |
|---|---|
| App management | View all apps with owner, status, cost; hibernate/wake/delete; transfer ownership; adjust resource tier |
| Team management | View all teams; per-team app count and cost; promote/demote quota tier; suspend a team |
| Cost and quotas | Total and per-team spend; budget alert thresholds; apps approaching quota ceiling; hibernate candidates |
| Platform health | Cluster status summary; failed deploy log; cert and DNS alerts; upgrade notifications |

### Routine operator cadence

Expected time investment is a few hours per month. No operator action is required for normal day-to-day developer activity.

- **Weekly:** glance at cost dashboard and new team digest
- **On request:** promote a team's quota tier when they hit their limit
- **On offboarding:** transfer app ownership when a team is dissolved
- **On alert:** investigate cert, DNS, or budget alerts

---

## 9. Hibernation

Apps that receive no traffic for their configured idle threshold are automatically scaled to zero replicas by KEDA. Persistence is retained. The app wakes transparently on the next HTTP request via the KEDA HTTP add-on, which holds the request while the pod starts.

| Property | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Idle detection | KEDA monitors HTTP request rate; zero requests for idle threshold triggers scale-to-zero |
| Wake-on-request | KEDA HTTP add-on holds the first request while the pod initialises |
| Cold start time | Typically 5–15 seconds depending on container image size |
| Persistence during hibernation | All data retained; no cleanup of database or storage |
| Worker hibernation | Workers scale to zero when their queue is empty (KEDA queue scaler) |
| CronJob hibernation | CronJobs suspended when app is hibernated; schedule resumes on wake |

---

| Requirement | Decision | Rationale |
|---|---|---|

| GitOps engine | Argo CD | Mature, well-supported, integrates cleanly with Kubernetes manifests. Pull-based model keeps cluster as source of truth. |
| Autoscale / hibernate | KEDA + KEDA HTTP add-on | Single tool handles queue-driven worker scaling and HTTP-driven hibernation. Scale-to-zero is native. |
| GitHub integration | Push model (GitHub calls Morsel) | OIDC tokens are short-lived, carry no org-level access, and require no credentials stored on either side. |
| App ownership | GitHub teams (not individuals) | Teams are stable across membership churn. Individual ownership requires operator action on every departure. |
| Team onboarding | Automatic with default quota | Manual onboarding is high operator burden. Automatic onboarding with a low default quota bounds cost exposure without blocking developers. |
| Quota tiers | Three tiers: default, standard, power | Coarse tiers are easier to explain and administer than per-app limits. Default auto-assigned; upper tiers require operator action. |
| Operator tooling | Custom admin UI (web, desktop) | Operator may rotate and has no K8s/GCP knowledge. kubectl and GCP console are not acceptable operator interfaces. |
| Persistence | GCS, Cloud SQL, Cloud Pub/Sub | Fully managed GCP services; no in-cluster databases to operate. One resource per app for isolation. |
| DNS / TLS | external-dns + cert-manager + Let's Encrypt | Fully automated; zero operator involvement in cert renewal or DNS record management. |
| Container registry | Private Artifact Registry, one repository per team | Keeps images private to the org. Workload Identity means no credentials stored in GitHub or Kubernetes. Per-team repositories prevent cross-team image overwrites. |

---

## 11. Open questions

These should be resolved before implementation of the relevant phase begins.

- What is the operator's notification channel? (Slack, email, or both?)
- What domain will Morsel manage? (e.g. `apps.internal.example.com`)
- Should the idle threshold be configurable per-app in `morsel.json`, or set platform-wide by the operator?
- How should database credentials be vended to apps? (Kubernetes Secrets, GCP Secret Manager, or both?)
- What is the GCP project naming convention and overall budget ceiling?
- Should the admin UI authenticate via GitHub OAuth (tying operator identity to org membership), or use a standalone credential?
- What is the process for the designer to push platform upgrades (GKE versions, Helm chart updates) with minimal operator disruption?

---

## 12. Iterative build plan

The platform is built incrementally. Each phase is independently useful and testable before the next begins.

| Phase | Scope |
|---|---|
| 1 — Foundation | GCP project, GKE cluster, Artifact Registry (with per-team repository structure), VPC, Terraform baseline |
| 2 — GitOps core | Argo CD, namespace-per-app scaffolding, basic `morsel.json` manifest rendering |
| 3 — Deploy API | Morsel API service, GitHub OIDC validation, image provenance check, team auto-registration, quota enforcement |
| 4 — Networking | GKE Gateway API, internal/external ingress, cert-manager, external-dns, custom domain |
| 5 — Persistence | GCS bucket provisioning, Cloud SQL vending, Pub/Sub topic creation, secret injection |
| 6 — Hibernation | KEDA, HTTP add-on, idle detection, scale-to-zero, wake-on-request |
| 7 — Admin UI | Operator web UI: app list, team management, quota promotion, cost dashboard |
| 8 — Hardening | Budget alerts, audit logging, disaster recovery runbook, operator handover docs |

Each phase will produce a working, reviewable increment. Design decisions specific to a phase will be captured as addenda to this document before that phase begins.
