{"language": "bash", "code": "cat > /mnt/user-data/outputs/morsel-conversation-transcript.md << 'TRANSCRIPT_EOF'
# Morsel — Design Conversation Transcript

> Compiled from conversation between designer and Claude · May 2026

---

## Opening

**User:** lets iteratively build our way up to a PAAS

I want to build a self host PAAS to host non-production apps (demo, experimental apps) in an enterprise environment.

The PAAS will probably be hosted in GCP in an account dedicated to non-production use

The PAAS apps should be language agnostic (Container implied)
The PAAS should provide the ability to run apps that are some combination of
* HTTP servers
* Workers
* Scheduled jobs

The PAAS must provide persistence for apps in the form of
* Blob storage
* Databases
* Queues

The PAAS must be able to make its apps unreachable from the public internet
The PAAS must be able to manage DNS and HTTPS for its apps (under some domain managed by the operator)
The PAAS must be able to wholly manage its apps via git ops (IAC implied)
The PAAS must be multi-user (the users are expected to be members of a private github org managed by the operator)

It must be low maintenance (part time maintenance for a single operator)
It must implement cost caps (implies quotas for individual users or apps)
It must be able to detect and hibernate apps that have not been used for a while
It must be able to transfer ownership of apps (as people leave the github org)

Let use these requirements as a starting point and gather more as we go

**Claude:** [Presented architecture diagram and asked clarifying questions]

**Q: How many apps and users are you expecting at steady state?**
**A: Large: ~50+ users, ~500+ apps**

**Q: How much GCP infrastructure complexity are you comfortable managing?**
**A: High: fine with full Kubernetes control plane**

**Q: How do developers deploy apps — what's your preferred GitOps model?**
**A: Push to git → auto deploy (Heroku-style)**

---

## Architecture overview

**Claude:** [Presented six-layer architecture: Developer experience, Control plane, GKE runtime, Persistence, Network/DNS/TLS, Identity/cost]

Good answers — these significantly clarify the architecture. Large scale + full K8s + Heroku-style DX points to a clear stack.

---

## Designer vs operator distinction

**User:** Small revision, I as the designer/implementer and comfortable with k8s complexity but want to hide that from the operator of this PAAS. It is a key requirement to achieve low maintenance

**Claude:** That's an important distinction — it reshapes the design philosophy significantly. The architecture stays the same underneath, but we need an operator-facing abstraction layer sitting above all that Kubernetes complexity. The operator should never need to write YAML, run kubectl, understand namespaces, or think about KEDA scalers.

[Presented persona split diagram: Designer / Operator / Developer with separate interface surfaces]

---

## GitHub teams as owners

**User:** lets make another design change, lets make the owners of apps github teams as those are more stable. the operator could rotate, mobile friendly access is not required, admin UI is preferred

**Claude:** Good call — GitHub teams as owners is strictly better. Teams survive individual org membership changes, have their own maintainers who can self-manage membership, and map cleanly to cost attribution.

[Presented team ownership model diagram showing lifecycle: member joins, member leaves, team dissolved]

---

## Security model — inverted trust

**User:** thinking through the security implications has made me change my mind about the model. We are going down a path that makes the PAAS a vector for exfiltrating github info. For the model to work the PAAS cannot afford to leak GH tokens or escalate privilege. The system is going to be too complicated to make those guarantees.

I think a better approach is to have github actions call PAAS APIs with PAAS tokens and push state changes into the PAAS

I still have to think a bit about how to model users in the PAAS and make sure they represent github teams

**Claude:** This is a really good security instinct. The inversion you're proposing is much cleaner: GitHub is the caller, not the called. The PaaS never holds a GitHub token. It only accepts signed, scoped attestations pushed to it.

[Presented inverted trust model diagram]

---

## Default quota model

**User:** can we get the low maintenance of option A and the gating of option C if we have default quotas that are applied to Apps without an explicit operator assigned quota?

**Claude:** Yes, exactly — and it's actually cleaner than Option C because there's no approval step to forget about or queue to drain. The model becomes: Every team gets in automatically. The default quota is just low enough that you can prove your app works, but not so generous that runaway costs are possible without operator awareness.

[Presented three quota tiers: Default (~$15/mo), Standard (~$80/mo), Power (~$300/mo)]

---

## Naming the project

**User:** lets name the project morsel. No need to mention the earlier design in the security model. lets rename paas.yaml to morsel.json

**Claude:** [Updated spec with Morsel branding throughout, renamed paas.yaml to morsel.json]

---

## Artifact Registry and credentials

**User:** lets flesh out the artifact registry a bit because it implies some credentials since the private org artifacts should not be in a public registry

**Claude:** [Explained push path via WIF, pull path via node pool service account, per-team repository structure]

**User:** what costs am I incurring here with the private registry? I really don't need very much registry functionality, I really just need the current image and the last healthy image to deploy in order to implement automatic rollback for failed deploys.

**Claude:** Storage is $0.10/GB/month. At demo/experiment scale very low. My recommendation is Option A — Artifact Registry with a 2-image retention policy per app.

**User:** What if morsel manages a fixed set of base images and apps only send the top-most layer consisting of the app code itself?

**Claude:** Interesting idea but the dependency layer problem means it probably doesn't eliminate the large-upload problem in practice. The staging repository approach is simpler.

---

## Staging handshake

**User:** not excited about it but sounds like the staging registry is the way to go. one last question how are credentials across the registries managed because as always I want the option to keep all of this off the public internet and I want to preserve the security model where compromising the PAAS does not compromise the operators larger infrastructure

**Claude:** [Explained push via WIF, pull via node pool service account, Private Google Access, self-hosted runners explicitly out of scope]

**User:** let stay with github actions but yes record all the other security decisions they are critical since this is a convenience service it cannot impact the wider security posture of the operator

**Claude:** Absolutely the right call — a convenience service that creates a security liability defeats its own purpose.

[Expanded security model with: GCP project isolation, IAM least-privilege table, staging handshake detail, full credential summary table showing nothing stored/nothing long-lived, Private Google Access, self-hosted runners explicitly out of scope]

---

## First spec document

**Claude:** [Produced morsel-design-spec.md v0.1 covering all decisions to date]

**User:** I'm much much rather a markdown document, it's far more portable

**Claude:** Good call — markdown is easier to version control alongside the code too.

[Produced markdown version of spec]

---

## Bootstrap binary

**User:** lets flesh out a bit more detail on the operator tooling and figure out tooling and initial setup. I would like the operator to be able to boot the stack with a single binary and an access token to a gcp project. I would like the operator bootstrap to be super simple and for the operator to be guided through a wizard if necessary

**Q: What should the bootstrap binary be written in?**
**A: Go — single static binary, easy to distribute, strong GCP SDK**

**Q: How should the binary be distributed to the operator?**
**A: GitHub Releases — operator downloads from a URL**

**Q: What should the operator provide as their GCP access?**
**A: OAuth flow launched by the binary itself**

**Claude:** [Designed four-phase bootstrap: GCP auth, preflight checks, wizard, provisioning]

---

## No Terraform dependency

**User:** Does this imply a terraform dependency for the operator binary?

**Claude:** No — and that's exactly the right thing to flag. The cleaner path is to not use Terraform at all. Use the GCP Go SDK directly. The binary talks to GCP APIs natively.

| Concern | Implementation |
|---|---|
| GCP resource provisioning | GCP Go SDK — compiled into binary |
| Kubernetes resource management | k8s.io/client-go — compiled into binary |
| Helm chart installs | Helm Go SDK — compiled into binary |
| GCP authentication | OAuth2 Go library + localhost callback — compiled into binary |

---

## CLI naming

**User:** Can we make the binary name morsel, the operator functionality under the 'service' sub command, and the bootstraping under the 'bootstrap' command?

**User:** I want the bootstrap invocation to be morsel service bootstrap

**Claude:** Even better — keeps everything under `morsel service` and makes the CLI shape consistent.

```
morsel service bootstrap install
morsel service bootstrap upgrade
morsel service operator add --principal morsel-operators@example.com
```

**User:** Do not include rejected alternatives in the spec

**User:** Do not include a rationale for the cli naming

---

## Install vs upgrade

**User:** Do we need both an install and an upgrade

**Claude:** Good question. The binary already knows whether Morsel is installed by checking for the state bucket. It can make that determination itself. A single command: `morsel service bootstrap` — no state found → runs wizard then provisions; state found → reads existing config, applies updates.

---

## State storage → Secret Manager

**User:** I thought we weren't using terraform, what do we need the state bucket for?

**Claude:** You're absolutely right. Without Terraform there's no state file. We do still need to persist wizard configuration between runs. That's a small JSON document — the right home is Secret Manager, stored as `morsel-bootstrap-config` alongside other platform secrets.

---

## Cheap database for Morsel

**User:** Second question, what is the cheapest database solution available. It seems like the service itself will not be very data heavy

**Claude:** SQLite is the right call. No managed service, no instance cost, essentially free. The Morsel API runs as a single replica (no horizontal scaling) with a GKE Persistent Volume. Single writer is guaranteed by design.

---

## Cloudflare DNS support

**User:** What if there is an option to go with an external dns provider like cloudflare

**Claude:** `external-dns` supports Cloudflare natively. The bootstrap wizard gains one question: DNS provider: Cloud DNS / Cloudflare. If Cloudflare: API token scoped to single zone stored in Secret Manager — the one case where a Morsel secret has reach outside the GCP project boundary.

---

## Cost analysis

**User:** What costs am I incurring here with the private registry?

**Claude:** [Provided cost breakdown — GKE nodes are highest cost at ~$145/mo for three e2-standard-4 nodes]

**User:** The gke nodes seem to be my highest cost. The morsel service itself should be a low usage control and provisioning plane what is the cheapest alternative

**Claude:** GKE Autopilot — you pay per pod resource request rather than per node. Hibernated apps have zero running pods — cost is zero. Platform control plane ~$17/month. Total floor ~$25-30/month.

**User:** With autopilot does that mean I don't pay for idle apps?

**Claude:** Yes, exactly. Hibernated apps are genuinely free on Autopilot.

---

## Dropping third-party components

**User:** Are there any options to go even cheaper?

**Claude:** Drop Argo CD, KEDA, cert-manager, external-dns — implement their functionality natively in the Morsel API. Platform floor drops to ~$15/month.

**User:** Drop 3rd party dependencies if they are going to raise costs by that much

**Claude:** [Removed Argo CD, KEDA, cert-manager, external-dns. Morsel API becomes single control plane binary handling manifest apply, hibernation, certificates, DNS]

---

## Portability

**User:** Since morsel is handling much of the provisioning and setup of apps and not so much on 3rd party components does this design map to an AWS or Azure implementation

**Claude:** Yes, cleanly. Each infrastructure concern has a direct equivalent on AWS and Azure. The one concern not covered: admin UI auth (IAP is GCP-native; Cloudflare Access is a cloud-agnostic alternative).

**User:** Add a portability note. We are not designing for portability but we don't want to close the door

---

## IAP for admin UI

**User:** Github app registration is simpler but adding a GitHub app to the trusted apps for a private enterprise is probably going to be too high friction. Are there any other options besides maintaining a username password

**Claude:** GCP Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP). Operator accesses admin UI via their Google account. No password, no GitHub app. Bootstrap binary sets up IAP binding automatically.

**User:** Is it possible to allow groups instead of individuals to be operators

**Claude:** Yes — IAP supports Google Groups as principals. Bind `roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor` to a Google Group. Operator rotation means adding/removing from the group — no Morsel involvement.

**User:** Is it possible to support both individuals and groups?

**Claude:** Yes, trivially — IAP treats both identically. Wizard accepts either form.

---

## Repo-based ownership model

**User:** With the current limitation it looks like we should drop the notion of teams and individuals as app owners and make the repo the owner. When a GitHub action token is exchanged for a morsel token we encode the repo as a claim. Anyone that can trigger the deploy action can deploy but only deploy the apps defined in that repo

**Claude:** That's an elegant simplification. The repo is a stable, unambiguous identity that Morsel can verify from the OIDC token without any GitHub API calls. OIDC token already contains `repository` claim as a standard field.

**User:** At that point do we need an owner entry in morsel.json? Can we just infer ownership from the repo that matches the developers token?

**Claude:** Yes, exactly right — `owner` field removed from morsel.json. Ownership is an emergent property of who deploys.

---

## Orphaned apps redefined

**User:** lets make a couple of small usability updates. The overall goal is apps belong to a repo, are owned by 1 repo admin, ownership is managed by the repo admin but the operator can step in in unusual circumstances.

[Several iterations on ownership transfer, claim workflow, eventually simplified to:]

**User:** Let's redefine orphaned apps as apps who's GitHub repo has been deleted or archived. We currently have no answer for how we detect this condition. Remove the behavior of orphaning an app older than 90 days

**Claude:** [Updated spec — orphaned defined as deleted/archived repo, no automated detection, honest about the open problem, stale apps list remains as manual tool]

---

## .morsel/ folder structure

**User:** The spec is wrong about a root morsel.json

**Claude:** [Updated spec — `.morsel/` folder with `*.morsel.json` files, one per app]

**Q: A repo can have multiple apps — how should multiple apps be declared?**
**A: a .morsel folder with *.morsel.json files**

**Q: What should the URL scheme look like for apps?**
**A: app-name.repo-slug.apps.example.com with unnamed app getting repo-slug directly**

**Q: How should the GitHub Actions workflow handle multiple apps in a repo?**
**A: Single workflow — deploys all apps in parallel**

---

## Token model

**User:** New plan. Operations against the API require a morsel token. There are a couple of endpoints that exchange an external token for a morsel token.

When we exchange a GitHub action token for a morsel token it should be a 10 min token

When we exchange an operators gcp oidc token for a morsel token it should be a 90 day token

**Claude:** Clean model. Two exchange endpoints:
```
POST /api/token/github-oidc    → 10 min Morsel token
POST /api/token/gcp-oidc       → 90 day Morsel token
```

**User:** Let's do a hybrid where access tokens contain the role but expire quickly (configurable, default to 15 mins). But can be refreshed and the refresh mints a new access token with up to date information like role.

**Claude:** Standard OAuth2 access/refresh token pattern. Access token: 15 min JWT, no DB lookup. Refresh token: 90 days, one DB hit per 15 min. Refresh token rotated on every use.

---

## App operations design

**Q: How should changes to persistence declarations in morsel.json be handled after an app already exists?**
**A: Declarative source of truth, destructive changes blocked by default unless overridden by a flag**

**Q: Should the API expose app logs?**
**A: Let's make observability an opt in feature**

**Q: What should app status expose?**
**A: Separate endpoints for status, deploy history, and resource utilization**

**Q: Should deploy and provisioning operations be synchronous or asynchronous?**
**A: Async with a retry-after header**

---

## Sync endpoint

**User:** thinking through the GitHub action deploying the apps 1 by 1 informs morsel about which apps were added or modified. The GitHub action probably needs to give morsel enough data for it to know what apps to delete

**Claude:** The deploy payload needs to include the complete set of apps declared in the repo at that commit. Morsel can then diff against its own records and delete anything no longer declared.
